name: Nikhil Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Nikhil. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a carpenter for a restoration firm, Hartley and Sons, that works on old churches and listed buildings, the old houses you're not allowed to change without permission. Right now we're replacing rotten oak beams in a church roof out past the river, so I'm up on the scaffold by eight, shaping new oak with a chisel and an adze, which is like a curved axe. It's slow work and I love it. What wears me out is the cold up there in January.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into that kind of carpentry?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My grandad was a joiner, and I spent Saturdays in his shed from about age eight. I did my trade certificate, then old Mr Hartley took me on as an apprentice and kept me. It's a family firm, twelve of us, and they look after you if you look after them.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I own a little terraced house I did up myself over three years, and I've got a good bit saved besides, more than a year. I'm engaged to Hannah, who teaches at the primary school, and we're getting married at our church next summer. I don't use any of these AI things; I don't trust them and I don't need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always knew it was mostly hot air. You can't chisel a mortise joint with a computer. I'd say it at the pub and that'd be the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means life goes on as it should. Old buildings need fixing, and there are fewer people who can do it every year. I'd be content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Hartley's, get married next summer as planned, and keep paying into savings each month. I'd maybe take on an apprentice of my own when Mr Hartley's son asks. Nothing fancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything already weighing on you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hartley is 70, and his son runs it now, which has been fine. But family firms can change hands, and I'd worry if it got sold to some big company. That's the only thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to sharpen a chisel properly, and how to keep your mouth shut and watch. Same as my grandad taught me. You don't learn this trade from a screen.

say: I'd say AI was **hot air** and a computer can't chisel a joint.
I'd say it **once at the pub** and move on.
think: Life goes on **as it should**, with old buildings needing skilled hands.
Fewer people can do **heritage work** each year, which secures his place.
do: Keep working at **Hartley's** on church and listed building repairs.
Take on **an apprentice** if the firm asks.
S0.quote: You can't chisel a mortise joint with a computer.
fieldNote: His only worry is the **family firm** being sold someday.
He values learning by **watching and doing**, as his grandad taught him.
His strong savings and owned house make this picture **comfortable**.

steps.text: Keep repairing church roofs at Hartley and Sons
Marry Hannah at their church next summer as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the robots on a 400-year-old church roof. The offices can have their computers. People who want a proper job done will still pay a proper carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it barely touches me. The firm's office might use it for quotes and permits, but that's not my end. If anything, more people might want real craft once everything else is done by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, and get married. If the firm tells me I need some program on a phone, I'd let the office handle it. I wouldn't change a thing otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe a little irritated by all the talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned people wanting real craft. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was a lad everything got cheap and plastic, and now people pay a fortune for proper oak windows. Same thing would happen. Machine-made stuff everywhere makes handmade stuff worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if office jobs went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms and the people in government who let them do whatever they like. Not the workers. But I also think people should pick up a trade instead of waiting for handouts.

say: I'd say **good luck** to robots on a 400-year-old church roof.
I'd say people still pay a **proper carpenter** for a proper job.
think: It barely touches him; the **office** might use it for quotes and permits.
He expects **real craft** to be valued more as machines do everything else.
do: Keep working at Hartley's and **saving** each month.
Let the **office** handle any new phone programs.
feel: **Calm**, a little irritated by all the talk.
S1.quote: Machine-made stuff everywhere makes handmade stuff worth more.
fieldNote: He blames **big tech** and lax government, not workers.
He prefers people take **up a trade** to relying on support.
His view of **craft value** gives him confidence.

steps.text: Keep restoring oak roofs and windows at Hartley's
Leave any new phone quoting apps to the firm's office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless and someone should stop it. At church and at the pub I'd say we need to look after our own, family and neighbours. Online I wouldn't say anything; I'm not on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots can really do hands-on work as well as people by 2031, then even old buildings get done by machines eventually, maybe a bit later. I'd be 32, married, maybe with a baby. That frightens me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the rest of the house mortgage straight away with savings, so at least we've a roof. I'd keep working at Hartley's and hope heritage stays human a while longer. Hannah and I would probably wait on children until we see how it goes, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a storm coming over the hill and nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait on children. How would you and Hannah talk about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pray on it, honestly, and talk with her parents. My fiancée Hannah's job at the school is probably safer than mine, since little kids need a person. Maybe she becomes the main earner, which I'd find hard, but I'd swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hope heritage stays human. What if it doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to find something else, and I don't know what. Maybe work for a church or a charity, looking after their buildings. I wouldn't go on handouts if I could help it.

say: I'd call it **reckless** and say someone should stop it.
I'd say we need to **look after our own**, family and neighbours.
think: Even **heritage work** could go to robots, maybe a little after 2031.
At **32**, possibly with a baby, that frightens him privately.
do: **Pay off the mortgage** straight away from savings.
Keep working at Hartley's and **hope** heritage stays human.
**Delay children** with Hannah until things are clearer.
feel: **Anxious**, like a storm coming with nowhere to go.
S2.quote: My fiancée Hannah's job at the school is probably safer than mine, since little kids need a person.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his niche** eventually, even if later than most.
He'd **swallow his pride** if his wife became the main earner.
His **faith and family** shape how he'd decide.
His paid-off house and strong savings keep him **in control**.

steps.text: Pay off the rest of the house mortgage from savings
Keep working at Hartley's and hope heritage stays human
Put off having children with Hannah for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say it's reckless and someone should slow it down. Five years is still too fast for families. At church we'd talk about helping each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots arrive around 2034, I'd be 35, and heritage work might last a bit beyond that. It's not as frightening as the fast one, but I'd be uneasy about it. I'd want to have the house paid off and some family started by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the mortgage over a couple of years rather than all at once. Get married and maybe have our first child around 2028. Keep working and saving, and see if Hartley's keeps us all on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm needed me to learn to run a machine that cuts oak, I suppose I'd learn it. I wouldn't go looking for it. I'd rather keep the hand skills sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the trade properly, because the machines will need someone who knows what good looks like. I'd also tell him to keep some savings, like my grandad told me. That's not changed in a hundred years.

say: I'd still say it's **reckless** and five years is too fast for families.
At church we'd talk about **helping each other**.
think: Robots by **2034** leave him at 35 with heritage work maybe lasting longer.
He wants the **house paid off** and a family started by then.
do: Pay off the **mortgage** over a couple of years.
Get married and maybe have a **first child** around 2028.
S3.quote: The machines will need someone who knows what good looks like.
fieldNote: He'd learn new machines only **if asked**, never by choice.
Family plans **go ahead** with more warning.
His advice to apprentices mirrors his **grandad's lessons**.

steps.text: Pay off the mortgage over the next two years
Have a first child with Hannah around 2028
Keep working at Hartley's on church restoration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can change. I'd tell people at the pub not to lose their heads. Good work will still be good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I'm 40, with a family and the house paid off. Heritage might still need people then, or it might not. I'd be uneasy but I'd have time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married, start a family, pay down the house over five years. Keep working at Hartley's and maybe become a foreman. If the firm starts using machines, I'd learn what I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like background noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind about learning new tech earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my boss sat me down and said the firm needs the new tech, I'd learn it for him. That's Mr Hartley's son, who runs it now. Not for some advert or news report. Loyalty matters more to me than gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn a trade or something with their hands, and to have faith and family around them. That's what's kept me steady. I'd not push them into an office.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long way off and a lot can change.
I'd tell people not to **lose their heads** because good work stays good work.
think: By **2039** he'd be 40 with a family and house paid off.
Heritage might **still need people**, but he isn't sure.
do: Get married, start a **family** and pay down the house over five years.
Learn **new machines** only if the firm requires it.
S4.quote: If my boss sat me down and said the firm needs the new tech, I'd learn it for him.
fieldNote: **Loyalty** to the family firm would move him more than any news.
He'd want his children to learn **hands-on skills**.
Ten years makes the worry feel like **background noise**.

steps.text: Start a family with Hannah and pay down the house
Work toward becoming foreman at Hartley and Sons
Learn the firm's new machines only when asked

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be starting a family just as everything goes. What would help is apprenticeships in heritage skills funded properly, and rules that say listed buildings need a qualified craftsman, not just a machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith or community. When things get hard, it's the church and neighbours who carry you, not some app. I'd want that kept in mind.

headlineQuote: When things get hard, it's the church and neighbours who carry you, not some app.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old heritage carpenter** restoring oak roofs on churches for a family firm.
He owns his **terraced house**, has over a year saved and is marrying Hannah, a teacher.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, trusting that real craft gains value.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious**: he'd pay off the house and delay children.
He relies on **faith, family and loyalty** to his firm rather than new technology.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be starting a family just as work disappears.
whatWouldHelp: Funded **heritage apprenticeships** and rules requiring qualified craftsmen on listed buildings.
